intro: Introduction to European Union Law. Lecture five: the sources of Union law, and their hierarchy.

slides.16: Accession, phase one: becoming a candidate. The steps in order. A third country submits an application to the Council. The Council notifies the European Parliament and the national parliaments, and consults the European Commission. The Parliament must give its consent. And then the Council decides. Only at the end of that sequence is the state a candidate country.
slides.17: The same sequence, now completed — the applicant has become a candidate country.
slides.22: Withdrawal: Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union, illustrated with the Brexit timeline from the Council's own site. The structure of the article: a member state may decide to withdraw in accordance with its own constitutional requirements; it notifies the European Council; the Union negotiates a withdrawal agreement, concluded by the Council by qualified majority with Parliament's consent; and the Treaties cease to apply from the date of entry into force of that agreement or, failing that, two years after notification, unless the European Council unanimously agrees to extend. That automatic two-year cliff is the provision's most important feature: it puts the pressure of time on the withdrawing state.
slides.23: General principles of Union law, and where they come from: the telos of the Treaties — their purpose and system — and the common legal tradition of the member states, with the Court of Justice confirming and shaping them through case law. And a question mark hangs over that last phrase, which is the standing criticism: the Court both finds and makes these principles.
slides.33: Tertiary law: two instruments sitting below secondary law — delegated acts under Article 290, and implementing acts under Article 291.
slides.48: The hierarchy, from the top down. Primary law. Then international agreements concluded by the Union. Then secondary law. Then tertiary law. And below all of it, member state law. Off to one side sits a bracket labelled the integration-proof core of the member states, with a question mark: the contested claim of national constitutional courts that some core of national constitutional identity stands outside this order. Note in particular the position of international agreements — below primary law, but above secondary law. Which means a Union act can be annulled for conflicting with an agreement the Union concluded.
slides.51: Any member state law — and the word to stress is any. Every level of Union law stands above every level of member state law, national constitutions included. That is the claim primacy makes, and the next lecture is devoted to it.
slides.53: Three limits in one picture, and they are the three ways a Union act can be attacked or resisted. Competence: did the Union have the power at all? Primacy, and its shadow, ultra vires: does Union law prevail, and what if a national court says the Union acted beyond its powers? And the integration-proof core: is there national constitutional ground that Union law cannot reach? The first is settled law. The second and third are the live constitutional conflict between the Court of Justice and the national constitutional courts.
